1. Core Clinical Tension: A 47-year-old immunocompetent male presents with subacute localized prepatellar swelling and antalgic gait lacking constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats) or respiratory complaints, masquerading as routine prepatellar bursitis or non-specific superficial soft tissue infection. The finding of focal cortical patellar erosion on knee radiographs and an asymptomatic pleural effusion on chest imaging creates diagnostic tension between pyogenic osteomyelitis and extrapulmonary skeletal tuberculosis.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs after baseline physical exam, systemic inflammatory markers, plain radiographs of the knee and chest, and diagnostic knee MRI, but strictly prior to operative surgical intervention, joint aspiration, intraoperative visualization of caseous tissue, and histopathologic analysis.
3. Differential Distinctions: Uncomplicated prepatellar bursitis and superficial cellulitis are ruled out by failure of standard anti-inflammatory and antibiotic therapy, elevated ESR (55 mm/hr), patellar cortical bone erosion, and reactive popliteal lymphadenopathy. Acute pyogenic bacterial osteomyelitis typically presents with acute severe pain, systemic toxicity, and neutrophilic bone destruction without caseation. Tuberculous patellar osteomyelitis is established by surgical curettage revealing caseous bone necrosis and histology demonstrating caseating granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated Langhans giant cells in conjunction with pleural effusion.
case_prompt:
A 47-year-old Indian male presents to the outpatient clinic with a 1-month history of sudden-onset left knee joint pain, swelling, and an antalgic gait. He reports limitation of motion, particularly during terminal flexion. He commutes daily by train, works in an office setting, and has no personal or family history of chronic pulmonary illness or known sick contacts. He denies preceding trauma, fever, night sweats, anorexia, weight loss, or respiratory symptoms. Prior to presentation, he was treated empirically by a primary care physician for a suspected superficial skin infection with oral antibiotics and anti-inflammatory medications, without symptomatic improvement.

On physical examination, the patient has localized swelling and tenderness over the prepatellar region of the left knee, accompanied by mild overlying erythema and local warmth compared to the right knee. There is no discharging sinus or skin breakdown. Range of motion of the left knee is terminally painful but otherwise preserved. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable.

Initial laboratory evaluation reveals mild normocytic anemia, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 55 mm/hr, and elevated qualitative C-reactive protein (CRP). Plain radiography of the left knee demonstrates focal cortical erosion along the anterior margin of the patella. Plain chest radiography reveals an old, healed left fifth rib fracture and blunting of the left costophrenic angle consistent with a left-sided pleural effusion. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left knee confirms focal osteomyelitis involving the anterior patella with cortical erosion, an associated fluid collection extending into the anteroinferior subcutaneous plane over the patellar tendon, a reactive joint effusion without intra-articular extension, and an enlarged popliteal lymph node.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Prepatellar bursitis was the initial working diagnosis due to localized anterior knee inflammation; however, failure to respond to two weeks of conservative therapy and antibiotics, along with radiographic demonstration of cortical bone erosion, excluded uncomplicated superficial bursitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A primary diagnosis of prepatellar bursitis was made, and anti-inflammatory medicines with empirical antibiotic coverage were prescribed. After two weeks of rest, ice application, and medical treatment, there was no significant relief of symptoms.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Post-traumatic or hematogenous bacterial osteomyelitis was considered due to anterior patellar erosion and surrounding fluid collection; however, the indolent course without high fevers or acute purulent sinus formation, coupled with intraoperative caseous necrosis rather than simple purulence, argued against typical pyogenic infection.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: According to the above-mentioned findings, infective bacterial post-traumatic osteomyelitis with prepatellar bursitis was the provisional diagnosis, and workup was done for surgery of excision biopsy, debridement

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnosis was confirmed by operative surgical curettage and histopathological examination, which identified friable bone tissue with caseous necrosis surrounded by histiocytes, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and multinucleated giant cells, corroborated by an incidental pleural effusion on chest imaging.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Intraoperatively, author found that the osteomyelitis showed friable necrotic tissue with caseous necrosis of bone... Histopathological examination of biopsied soft tissue and bony material showed necrotic areas surrounded by histiocytes, variable lymph plasma cells, neutrophils and occasional multinucleated giant cells without signs of malignancy

editor_comments: Stanford MedCaseReasoning distillation completed. The admission prompt terminates before joint aspiration and operative debridement, withholding the intraoperative caseous necrosis and histopathology.
